readme.html: Module 10: Monitoring, Compliance, and Governance in the AWS Cloud

readme.title: What this module covers
readme.html:
What this module covers

This module follows the path that starts with securing AWS resources and moves through monitoring and auditing to compliance and governance. It introduces Amazon CloudWatch for metrics, alarms, dashboards and logs, and AWS CloudTrail for auditing every API call. It then covers compliance tools (AWS Artifact, AWS Config, AWS Audit Manager), multi-account governance (AWS Organizations, AWS License Manager, AWS Control Tower, AWS Service Catalog), and finally AWS Health, AWS Trusted Advisor and IAM Access Analyzer.

readme.title: Lessons
readme.html:
Lessons

Module 10 Introduction

  1. Introduction to Monitoring, Compliance, and Governance in the AWS Cloud: the secure, monitor, audit, comply progression.

Monitoring and Compliance Services

  1. Introduction to Monitoring: what monitoring is and why dynamically scaling resources need it.
  2. Amazon CloudWatch: metrics, alarms, dashboards and logs, told through espresso machines.
  3. AWS CloudTrail: auditing every API call with events, logs and Insights.
  4. Compliance: what AWS covers for you, AWS Artifact and the Customer Compliance Center.
  5. Auditing AWS Resources for Compliance: AWS Config for configuration rules and AWS Audit Manager for evidence.
  6. AWS Organizations: consolidated billing, OUs and SCPs across many accounts.
  7. Governance: Control Tower, Service Catalog and License Manager for governing accounts, resources and licenses.
  8. AWS Health: account-specific health events through the AWS Health Dashboard.
  9. AWS Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks in five categories, plus IAM Access Analyzer.

readme.title: Key takeaways
readme.html:
Key takeaways

  • Work through securing, monitoring, auditing, then compliance and governance.
  • CloudWatch watches AWS and on-premises resources with metrics, threshold alarms (SNS notifications or automatic scaling), self-refreshing dashboards and central logs.
  • CloudTrail records who made each API call, when, from where and with what result, keeping 90 days of event history for free and longer-term logs in S3.
  • AWS Artifact is the no-cost source of AWS audit reports and agreements with AWS.
  • Customer stories, key compliance answers and the auditing checklist live in the Customer Compliance Center (the AWS Compliance portal), not in Artifact.
  • AWS Config checks resource configurations against your rules, while AWS Audit Manager automates the evidence that proves compliance.
  • AWS Organizations consolidates billing and groups accounts into OUs, and SCPs cap permissions for OUs or member accounts, never for IAM users, groups or roles.
  • AWS Control Tower governs multi-account setups through a landing zone, Account Factory, controls and a dashboard.
  • Service Catalog offers curated self-service resources, and License Manager tracks software licenses, including BYOL.
  • AWS Health reports events that affect your resources, Trusted Advisor checks against best practices, and IAM Access Analyzer refines permissions toward least privilege.

readme.title: What the assessment focuses on
readme.html:
What the assessment focuses on

The assessment has 11 questions, and each bullet says how many include the concept as an option or topic and how many expect it as the answer, then the cue that points to it.

  • Amazon CloudWatch (in 4, answer in 1): metrics, threshold alarms and automatic EC2 scaling.
  • AWS CloudTrail (in 5, answer in 1): who changed what and when, across cloud and on premises.
  • AWS Artifact (in 7, answer in 1): no-cost, on-demand AWS reports and agreements, and nothing else.
  • AWS Trusted Advisor (in 5, answer in 1): continuous checks and advice on cost, performance, security and resilience.
  • AWS Organizations (in 4, answer in 1): one rolled-up bill and accounts grouped into OUs.
  • Service control policies (in 1, answer in 1): the Organizations feature that caps the services, resources and API actions users can reach, distinct from the root, OUs and IAM users.
  • AWS Service Catalog (in 3, answer in 1): a curated, self-service set of approved resources.
  • AWS License Manager (in 2, answer in 1): BYOL licenses, usage limits and noncompliance risk.
  • AWS Control Tower (in 2, answer in 1): the landing zone as the container for everything you regulate.
  • AWS Config (in 1, answer in 1): configuration guidelines and approved instance lists, with Audit Manager, Artifact and CloudTrail as traps.
  • Customer Compliance Center (in 1, answer in 1): the assessment's name for the AWS Compliance portal of stories, key compliance answers and the auditing checklist, with Artifact (reports and agreements only) as the trap.
  • AWS Health (in 1, never the answer): a look-alike for Service Catalog.
  • Earlier-module concepts (in 4, never the answer): Availability Zones, the AWS Management Console, security groups, VPCs, subnets and IAM users as distractors.

readme.title: Summary
readme.html:
Summary

The module reads as a chain: secure first, then watch, then record, then prove, then govern. CloudWatch does the watching with metrics, alarms and dashboards, and CloudTrail keeps the record of every API call. Proof comes from AWS Artifact for AWS's side and from Config and Audit Manager for yours. Governance scales through Organizations, Control Tower, Service Catalog and License Manager, while Trusted Advisor keeps reviewing cost, security, performance and more across the whole estate.

Basis

Four steps

Introduction to Monitoring

Objectives

  • Define cloud and what it gains you.

Notes

Definition

  • Monitoring constantly gathers, charts and tracks how healthy and fast your AWS infrastructure, services and apps run.
  • Its goal is peak performance and early warning of problems.
  • The loop: watch, gather metrics, judge them over time, then act.

Coffee shop metrics

  • The owner cannot watch all day, so wants a report (coffees sold, average wait, stock-outs) and an alert when waits run long.

Why the cloud needs it

  • AWS services scale on their own, so you must keep checking they behave.
  • AWS tools measure performance, warn when something is off, and help debug and troubleshoot.
  • With observability, it underpins reliability, availability, performance and security.
  • It uses live tools, dashboards, and log gathering and analysis.

Visuals

  • Benefits image: a locked badge, a geared clock for saved time, and a cloud with sliders.

Key takeaways

  • Monitoring means collecting metrics, judging them and acting.
  • makes it essential on AWS.
  • It can trigger automatic actions or alert people.

Scenarios

  • An overloaded : EC2 Auto Scaling launches another.
  • An error spike in an app: staff get notified.

Terms

  • Monitoring: ongoing tracking of resource health and performance.
  • Metric: a value tracked over time for a resource or process, such as EC2 CPU use or coffees sold.

Amazon CloudWatch

Objectives

  • Explain what offers and when to use it.

Notes

One place to watch

  • Amazon CloudWatch is a single real-time hub for watching AWS resources, the apps on them, and on-premises servers.
  • It shows resource usage, app performance and operational health system-wide.

Four features

Feature Job Coffee shop
Metrics Track a value per resource, built in (EC2 CPU) or custom Espresso Count, since machines need cleaning every 1,000 shots
Alarms Act when a crosses a threshold: notify, or change resources At 1,000, text the manager via
Dashboards Custom console pages, one view, near real time, self-refreshing Every machine's count on one screen
Logs Collect, store and monitor log files centrally; view, search, filter Why did machine two brew decaf last week?
  • Custom alarms work on metrics from any AWS resource type.

Why teams pick it

  • One integrated view replaces siloed monitoring.
  • Faster fixes (lower ) and better free developers for business work.
  • Pooled data yields insight, such as fleet-wide EC2 usage.
  • It also aids visualizing, automating and proactive monitoring; the core use is infrastructure troubleshooting.
  • Content delivery, purchase prediction and architecture design are other services' jobs, not CloudWatch's.

Visuals

  • Features graphic: a technician unsure how to watch it all, then one box per feature.

Key takeaways

  • CloudWatch monitors AWS and on-premises resources in real time from one place.
  • Metrics measure, alarms react, dashboards display, Logs keeps searchable detail.
  • An alarm can notify through SNS or scale EC2 automatically.
  • Choose it for performance numbers and thresholds, not for who called an .

Scenarios

  • Machines due for cleaning: a custom metric plus an alarm.
  • A machine brewed decaf: search .
  • A retailer's EC2 app stays overloaded: metrics and app logs, an alarm that adds instances, one dashboard.

  • Amazon CloudWatch: real-time monitoring for AWS resources and apps.
  • Metric: a value tracked over time for a resource or process, such as EC2 CPU use or coffees sold.
  • CloudWatch alarm: a metric threshold that triggers an action.
  • CloudWatch dashboard: a self-refreshing console page of metrics.
  • CloudWatch Logs: central log storage and search.
  • Amazon SNS: notification service that alarms use to send texts.
  • MTTR: mean time to resolution.
  • TCO: total cost of ownership.

aws-cloudtrail.html:
AWS CloudTrail

Objectives

  • Explain why auditing matters and what CloudTrail events, logs and Insights do.

Notes

Why auditing is easier on AWS

  • On premises, changes can slip by unrecorded, even accidental ones.
  • On AWS every action is an call, so all can be logged centrally.

What CloudTrail answers

  • Who called, when, from which IP, and the result: a new state or a denial.
  • Every request counts, from launching EC2 to editing permissions.
  • It also tracks activity on premises and with other cloud providers.
  • It eases audits, proves compliance, improves security posture and aids troubleshooting.
  • Integrity validation exposes tampering, and a separate log account blocks root-level edits.

Events, logs and Insights

Feature What it is
Events Single actions (API or console calls); shows 90 days of management events per Region, free, searchable, downloadable, unchangeable
Logs The files holding events, sent to S3 or , no 90-day cap, usable as or proof
Insights Studies management events for normal API volume and error rates, and flags deviations once enabled on a trail or event data store
  • CloudWatch Logs watches app internals, while CloudTrail records API activity.

Visuals

  • Hero: the who, what and when question CloudTrail exists to answer, across a and AWS.
  • Feature images: a phone alert, trails into a log, trend charts.

Key takeaways

  • CloudTrail answers who did what, when, where, and with what result.
  • Event history is free for 90 days, while S3 logs serve long audits.
  • Insights flags unusual API activity.

Scenarios

  • A hybrid financial firm traces changes for fixes and compliance: CloudTrail.
  • API activity files kept in S3 for audits: , not events or Insights.

Terms

  • AWS CloudTrail: audit log of AWS API calls.
  • Event history: free 90-day view of management events.
  • CloudTrail logs: event files stored in S3.
  • CloudTrail Insights: spots abnormal API activity.
  • Log file integrity validation: reveals tampered logs.
  • PCI: Payment Card Industry regulations.

compliance.html:
Compliance

Objectives

  • Define compliance and AWS's part in it.
  • Describe and its two types.
  • Find AWS compliance resources.

Notes

What compliance asks

  • It is a security and data-protection bar: your resources and data must satisfy each internal policy, industry standard and regulation that binds you.
  • Audits check this against documents, records and inspections.
  • Rules follow the workload: for EU consumer data, for US healthcare apps.
  • You need tools to gather records and inspect your AWS setup.

What AWS covers

  • You inherit AWS's best-practice data centers, networks, policies, processes and newest security controls.
  • AWS meets a long list of assurance programs, checked by outside auditors against thousands of requirements.
  • So you focus on your own workloads, helped by automated compliance and on-demand reports.
  • Bottom line: the infrastructure "of" the cloud is secure.

Regions and your data

  • Pick a Region in the right country for residency laws, since AWS never copies data across Regions unasked.
  • Per the , you own and control your data.
  • Encryption varies by service: use built-in features or build your own, and protection is often one resource setting.

AWS Artifact

  • A free portal that hands you AWS's own audit reports whenever needed and lets you handle certain online agreements.
  • Agreements: where you read, sign and track your agreements with AWS, for a single account or across , including HIPAA ones.
  • Reports: up-to-date outside audits of AWS against worldwide, regional and industry security rules, which you can show your auditors or regulators as proof.
  • It saves time, scales and lets you deploy with more confidence.
  • It does not group accounts or set SCPs (AWS Organizations) or create users ().

Where to learn more

  • The AWS Compliance portal (the video's AWS Compliance Center, the assessment's ) shows compliance-enabling services in one place.
  • It holds stories of regulated firms solving compliance, governance and audit problems.
  • Its whitepapers cover key compliance questions, a risk and compliance overview, and an auditing security checklist.
  • See also AWS Compliance Programs, the AWS Risk and Security whitepaper, and Additional compliance resources.

Visuals

  • AWS Artifact graphic: the service split into Agreements and Reports.

Key takeaways

  • You inherit AWS's compliant infrastructure and handle your own workloads.
  • Region choice keeps data where the law wants it.
  • AWS Artifact gives no-cost, on-demand reports and agreements.
  • Stories, key answers and the audit checklist live in the Customer Compliance Center, not Artifact.

Scenarios

  • Data must stay in its country: a Region there.
  • Signing an agreement with AWS: Artifact Agreements.
  • A developer needs their regulatory duties: Artifact Reports.

Terms

  • GDPR: EU General Data Protection Regulation.
  • HIPAA: US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996.
  • AWS Artifact: no-cost portal for AWS compliance reports and agreements.
  • AWS Artifact Agreements: the part of Artifact for signing and tracking agreements with AWS.
  • AWS Artifact Reports: third-party audit reports on AWS.
  • Customer Compliance Center: the AWS Compliance portal of stories, whitepapers and checklists.

auditing-aws-resources-for-compliance.html:
Auditing AWS Resources for Compliance

Objectives

  • Explain what and offer and when to use each.

Notes

AWS Config: do my resources follow our rules?

  • Firms set configuration rules per resource and must audit against them.
  • AWS Config records configurations, tracks changes and checks them against your rules.
  • It alerts you to noncompliant resources and can fix them automatically.
  • It reports pass and fail and keeps watching so settings stay put, as compliance is ongoing.
  • Uses: desired-state checks, ongoing security audits, troubleshooting, change management.

AWS Audit Manager: can I prove it?

  • Regulated firms must also prove it, as a financial firm must show it handles money safely.
  • Audit Manager is fully managed, audits usage continually and automates evidence collection across teams.
  • It tests whether controls (policies, procedures, activities) work, runs stakeholder reviews and builds audit-ready reports.
  • Prebuilt frameworks map your resources to standards and regulations.
  • Read-only access protects audit integrity, and it supports internal risk assessments.

Telling them apart

  • Only Config evaluates configurations: Audit Manager gathers evidence, AWS CloudTrail records calls, and AWS Artifact serves AWS's own audit reports.

Visuals

  • Audit Manager image: automation gathers evidence so two audit teams finish easily.

Key takeaways

  • Config checks configurations against your rules and can auto-fix.
  • Audit Manager automates evidence and offers prebuilt frameworks.
  • Configuration guidelines point to Config, even when cost is mentioned.

Scenarios

  • Developers must use only an approved, low-cost list of EC2 types: AWS Config.
  • A healthcare firm must show patient data is safe: Audit Manager.

Terms

  • AWS Config: evaluates resource configurations against rules.
  • Config rule: a standard Config checks resources against.
  • Automated remediation: fixes that restore compliance.
  • AWS Audit Manager: automates audit evidence collection.
  • Control: a policy, procedure or activity an audit tests.
  • Framework: prebuilt mapping of resources to a standard.

aws-organizations.html:
AWS Organizations

Objectives

  • Explain what is good for and when to use it.
  • Describe how its key concepts fit together.

Notes

The multi-account problem

  • One account suits early tests, but growing firms add accounts for production, non-production, developers or infrastructure.
  • Each may allow only some services and have its own customizations.
  • Managing them by hand fails, so AWS Organizations centralizes it.

What it gives you

  • One place to run billing, access, security and compliance for all accounts, and to share resources between them.
  • : child bills roll up to the parent account, where discounts apply.
  • Grouping: OUs gather accounts by security, compliance or budget needs, such as a developer OU.
  • Limits: the parent account's admin picks the services and actions each account gets.
  • Automation: programmatic account creation, cost control across accounts, tooling for security teams.
  • Adopt it early, before stray accounts pile up.

How the pieces fit

Piece What it is Where it sits
Top container, made with the organization Holds all OUs and accounts
Creates and governs the organization The owner
OU Logical group of accounts Holds accounts or nested OUs
Any other account In an OU, or under the root and still billed jointly
Cap on services, resources and API actions for an account's users and roles On an OU or one member account
  • SCPs never attach to users, groups or roles, even though they limit them.
  • Base OUs on each department's business, security and regulatory needs.
  • Careful: one assessment explanation calls the root the creating account, but the lesson keeps root (container) and management account (owner) apart.

Visuals

  • Hierarchy graphic: an org chart labeling the root, management account, OU, SCP and a member account outside any OU.

Key takeaways

  • Organizations centrally manages many accounts, including one consolidated bill.
  • OUs group accounts and can nest.
  • SCPs cap permissions and attach only to OUs or member accounts.

Scenarios

  • Accounts limited to regulation-approved services: one shared OU.
  • An account that fits no OU: directly under the root.

Terms

  • AWS Organizations: central management for many AWS accounts.
  • Consolidated billing: one combined bill for all accounts.
  • Organizational unit (OU): a logical group of accounts.
  • Service control policy (SCP): a permission cap for an OU or member account.
  • Management account: the owner account that sets up the organization and has final control.
  • Root: the organization's top container.
  • Member account: a child account billed through the management account.

governance.html:
Governance

Objectives

  • Explain when to use , and .

Notes

Why governance

  • Growth makes accounts, services and licenses harder to keep in check.
  • means rules that keep building and running a deployment efficient and aligned with business goals.
  • Cloud Town: a booming city's mayor lets builders act alone but enforces rules, like a height cap for a planned airport.
  • On AWS, a rule might require department tags for costs, though any root user could in theory ignore it.

AWS Control Tower

  • It is Cloud Town's control room: one place to apply security, operations and compliance rules to every account and organization, however many.
  • It matters more as builders multiply and setup grows complex.
  • Blueprints automate setup, including federated access management and account provisioning workflows.
  • Its four parts:
    • : the outer, best-practice multi-account boundary; every OU, account, user and resource you want under compliance rules lives inside it.
    • : stamps out each new account from one configurable template.
    • : high-level rules, like road crash barriers, that block nonconforming deployments and catch and fix noncompliant accounts and resources.
    • Dashboard: an ongoing visual summary of provisioned accounts, controls and compliance status.
  • Preconfigured controls speed multi-account setup, automate governance and integrate third-party software, saving time and adding control.
  • Use it to ship apps fast and issue compliant accounts, whether new to AWS, building an environment or launching a cloud initiative.

AWS Service Catalog

  • Fielding every request is slow, but staff guessing at settings is worse.
  • It lets you build, share and organize a curated catalog of approved resources, such as baseline networking and security tools for new accounts, for consistent governance.
  • Staff self-serve quickly and stay agile across accounts.
  • Uses: cross-account provisioning, access controls, faster pipelines.
  • It governs resources, while Control Tower governs account creation.

AWS License Manager and BYOL

  • Leaving on premises means deciding what to do with existing licenses.
  • reuses vendor-bought licenses (Microsoft, say) on EC2 or , flexibly and often far cheaper than AWS-bought ones.
  • License Manager tracks and controls those licenses and tunes their cost.
  • It curbs noncompliance with usage caps, blocked launches and other controls.
  • It also eases Microsoft License Mobility through Software Assurance and automates entitlement rollout across accounts.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, SQL Server on Amazon EC2 licensing With the Bring Your Own License (BYOL) model you reuse licenses you already own on AWS, while with included licenses, such as Server license-included instances on , AWS supplies the license and handles its cost and compliance.

Visuals

  • Control Tower graphic: the tower's dashboard oversees, Account Factory builds accounts with controls, a truck delivers them to the landing zone.
  • License image: an employee sure they own a license they cannot find.
  • Flashcards: one line each on the three services.

Key takeaways

  • Governance keeps cloud work efficient and aligned with company goals.
  • Control Tower builds and polices a governed multi-account environment, with the landing zone as its outer boundary.
  • Service Catalog offers curated, approved self-service resources.
  • License Manager tracks licenses, enforces limits and supports BYOL.

Scenarios

  • Staff unsure which resources to launch: Service Catalog.
  • Microsoft licenses moving to EC2 Dedicated Hosts: BYOL plus License Manager.
  • A government agency wants each new account to meet approved requirements: Control Tower, not CloudTrail (records calls) or License Manager (licenses).

Terms

  • Governance: rules keeping cloud work efficient and goal-aligned.
  • AWS Control Tower: builds and polices a governed multi-account environment.
  • Landing zone: the governed boundary around OUs, accounts, users and resources.
  • Account Factory: one template for every new account.
  • Controls (guardrails): high-level governance rules.
  • AWS Service Catalog: curated catalog of approved resources.
  • AWS License Manager: manages software licenses and their cost.
  • BYOL: using vendor-bought licenses on AWS.

aws-trusted-advisor.html:
AWS Trusted Advisor

Objectives

  • Explain what checks and how to act on its findings.
  • Explain how supports least privilege.

Notes

An automated advisor

  • Businesses gain from an outside expert who knows best practices and spots waste, savings and open security gaps.
  • AWS Trusted Advisor is that expert, automated: it runs live best-practice checks across your account.
  • Its checks fall into five categories: security, , performance, service limits and .
  • The callout states the same scope as optimizing cost, performance, security and resilience.
  • Results appear by category in the , and email alerts can reach billing, operations and security contacts.
  • Some checks come with every account and more depend on your support plan: dozens on all plans, hundreds from Business Support up.
  • Optimization is ongoing: turn Trusted Advisor on and act on its prioritized advice to optimize at scale.

Example checks

  • Status colors: red for action recommended, orange for investigation recommended, green for no problem found.
Category Checks Why it matters
Cost optimization Idle RDS instances, and EBS utilization, underused EC2 Scale down or delete what is flagged
Performance EBS volumes held back by their 's throughput -
Security Root user without , security groups open to the public Exposed resources are at risk
Fault tolerance EBS volumes without snapshots, EC2 not balanced across AZs, S3 buckets without proper logging No backup means lost data, and one failing AZ or instance can disrupt the app
Service limits Usage near or at a limit Many are soft limits, raised through the Service Quota console

IAM Access Analyzer

  • Trusted Advisor checks security broadly, but fine-grained permissions need IAM Access Analyzer.
  • It analyzes external access and checks policies against corporate security standards, so you can set, verify and refine permissions.
  • It validates and auto-reviews IAM policies, shows who can access what, and trims unused or overly broad access toward least privilege.

Look-alikes

  • scans for software vulnerabilities, the splits duties, and IAM Access Analyzer sets permissions, so none evaluates cost, security and performance.

Key takeaways

  • Trusted Advisor continuously checks your account against best practices in five categories.
  • For ongoing cost, security and performance advice, pick Trusted Advisor over Inspector or IAM Access Analyzer.
  • Your support plan sets how many checks you get.
  • IAM Access Analyzer refines IAM permissions toward least privilege.

Scenarios

  • A multi-Region enterprise wants ongoing cost, security and performance reviews plus best practices: Trusted Advisor.
  • EC2 instances crowded into one AZ: spread them across AZs so one failure cannot halt the app.

Terms

  • AWS Trusted Advisor: automated best-practice checker for accounts.
  • Soft limit: a service limit that can be raised to a degree.
  • EBS snapshot: a backup of an EBS volume.
  • IAM Access Analyzer: sets, verifies and refines IAM permissions.
  • Least privilege: granting only the access actually needed.
  • Amazon Inspector: scans workloads for software vulnerabilities.

lines: Each AWS action is an API call, so CloudTrail can show who made it, when, from which IP and with what result.
A denied call changed nothing, so it names neither who removed the bucket nor the last change made to it.
The source IP belongs to each call, so read it on the delete itself and not on an earlier sign-in.
CloudWatch Logs watches what happens inside apps, while CloudTrail records the API activity on the account.

questions.takeaway: To learn who made a change, when and from where, look to CloudTrail's record of API calls.

read.text: Who called, when, from which IP, and the result: a new state or a denial.

questions.stem: A security group rule on the cafe's loyalty database vanished overnight. The manager wants to know which user removed it, at what time and from which IP address. Which service answers this?

options.why: CloudTrail records each API call with the caller, the time, the source IP and the result.
AWS Config tracks resource settings and checks them against rules, not the caller and source IP of each request.
Control Tower sets up and governs a multi-account environment, so it does not answer who made one call.
CloudWatch watches metrics and application logs, not the identity behind each API request.

questions.takeaway: Changes that slip by unrecorded on premises become traceable on AWS because each one is a loggable API call.

read.text: On premises, changes can slip by unrecorded, even accidental ones.

questions.stem: In the cafe's old back-office server room, a staffer once changed a setting by mistake and nobody could ever trace it. After the move to AWS, what makes a slip like that traceable?

options.text: Each action on AWS goes through an API call
options.why: Even an accidental change is an API request on AWS, so it lands in the central activity record.

options.text: AWS takes care of the physical server hardware
options.why: AWS does run the hardware, but that shift in duties does not record who changed a setting.

options.text: IAM can limit each staffer to only needed rights
options.why: Tighter permissions can make slips less likely, but they leave no trace of a slip that still happens.

options.text: Staff sign in with multi-factor authentication
options.why: A second sign-in factor proves who logged in, yet on its own it does not record the setting they altered.

questions.takeaway: To dig into what a system did in the past, search the detailed records kept in CloudWatch Logs.

read.text: A machine brewed decaf: search CloudWatch Logs.

questions.stem: Last week one of the cafe's smart espresso machines brewed decaf when a customer ordered regular. The machines send their event records to AWS. Where should the team search to find out what happened?

options.why: A dashboard displays metric graphs, not the searchable event records needed to trace one brew.
CloudWatch Logs stores log files centrally so the team can search and filter last week's entries.
An alarm reacts to a metric threshold going forward; it holds no record of past events.
A metric holds numeric values over time, not the detailed record of what each brew did.

labs.title: Does the SCP allow it?
labs.brief: Market shop manager Raj cannot open the menu files even though his own policy allows it, and developer Kim cannot start a forecast training job in the test kitchen account. Switch statements on or off until every case gets its expected result. In this lab, an action needs an Allow from the SCPs at the root, at the OU and at the account and from the identity's own policies, an SCP grants nothing by itself, and an explicit Deny beats any Allow.

policies.label: Full access for the harbour shop
Full access for the market shop

cases.label: Raj opens today's drinks menu file
Raj saves a market stall order
Kim starts the latte forecast training job
Kim reads last month's test sales
Raj starts a forecast training job in the market shop
Raj deletes the market orders table

goals.label: Raj reads the menu and saves orders
goals.hint: Ask which level of the organization still says no once Raj's own policy says yes.

goals.label: Kim runs her forecast work in the test kitchen
goals.hint: Ask what Kim's own policy allows, since an SCP only sets the most an account may do.

goals.label: The shops keep to their approved services and keep their tables
goals.hint: Ask how far each Allow on the shops OU reaches, and what an explicit Deny does to an identity that may do anything to its tables.

lines: Raj's read went through only once the root, the shops OU and the market shop account all allowed Amazon S3, and his own policy did too.
An SCP caps what an account may do and grants nothing, so Kim still needed an Allow in her own identity policy.
Raj's forecast job stays blocked even though his policy allows it, because the shops' approved services leave it out.
The Deny on the shops OU stops table deletes in every shop account, whatever an identity policy allows.

questions.takeaway: To cap what whole accounts in an OU can use, attach a service control policy to that OU.

read.text: Service control policy (SCP): a permission cap for an OU or member account.

questions.stem: The cafe wants every account in its developer OU kept away from all but a handful of services, even for admins inside those accounts. What should it attach to the OU?

options.why: IAM policies attach to identities within one account, not to an OU of accounts.
A Config rule checks resource settings after the fact; it does not cap which services an account may call.
A budget alert warns about spending and blocks no service or API action.
An SCP on the OU caps the services and API actions for every user and role in its accounts, admins included.

questions.takeaway: Accounts with the same regulatory limits belong together in one shared OU.

read.text: Accounts limited to regulation-approved services: one shared OU.

questions.stem: Three of the cafe's accounts handle card payments and must stick to services a regulator has approved. What should the cafe do in AWS Organizations so that a single policy attachment caps all three, plus any payment account it adds later?

options.text: Attach one SCP to the organization root
options.why: A policy on the root would reach every account in the organization, not just the payment accounts.

options.text: Attach one SCP to each of the three accounts
options.why: Separate SCPs on each account work, but that is three attachments and a new payment account would need its own.

options.text: Place the three accounts in one shared OU
options.why: An OU groups accounts with the same regulatory needs, so one policy on it covers all three and any account moved in later.

options.text: Link the three accounts by consolidated billing
options.why: Consolidated billing combines charges into one bill, but it places no cap on which services an account may use.

questions.takeaway: An IAM policy grants nothing until it is attached to a user, group or role.

read.text: It only takes effect once attached to a user, group or role.

questions.stem: The cafe wrote a JSON policy that allows listing the reports bucket, yet staff still cannot list it. Which fact about policies explains this?

options.text: A policy has no effect until it is attached
options.why: A policy does nothing until it is attached to a user, group or role, so staff gain nothing yet.

options.text: A policy can hold both Allow and Deny rules
options.why: This is true, but the policy only allows, so mixing rule types does not explain the problem.

options.text: A policy can cover just a single S3 bucket
options.why: This is true, and the policy is scoped to the reports bucket, which is the one staff want to list.

options.text: A policy is written as a JSON document
options.why: This is true of every policy, so it does not explain why this one grants nothing yet.

incidents.title: The lunch rush that slowed the ordering app
incidents.brief: On Saturday the cafe's online ordering app slowed to a crawl in the middle of the lunch rush, and the owner wants to know what went wrong and how to keep it from happening next weekend.

steps.takeaway: A value CloudWatch tracks over time for a resource, such as EC2 CPU use, is a CloudWatch metric.

read.text: Metric: a value tracked over time for a resource or process, such as EC2 CPU use or coffees sold.

steps.stem: The cafe's ordering app runs on Amazon EC2 instances, and the team wants to see whether their CPU use climbed during the lunch rush. Nobody has set up anything custom in Amazon CloudWatch yet. Which CloudWatch feature already tracks that value over time?

options.why: An alarm reacts when a value crosses a threshold, and it needs a tracked value to watch in the first place.
A metric tracks a value over time for a resource, and EC2 CPU use is one CloudWatch tracks out of the box.
Logs collects and searches log files, while the CPU figure over time is kept as a metric.
A dashboard only displays values on one page, and the CPU figure it would show is tracked as a metric.

steps.takeaway: To act on its own when a metric crosses a threshold, such as adding EC2 capacity, use a CloudWatch alarm.

read.text: CloudWatch alarm: a metric threshold that triggers an action.

steps.stem: CPU use on the cafe's ordering servers stays high for most of every lunch rush. The owner wants another EC2 instance added on its own as soon as CPU passes a set level, with no one watching a screen. Which Amazon CloudWatch feature should set that off?

options.why: A dashboard shows the CPU figures on one page, but someone still has to watch it and act.
A Logs query searches stored log files on request, and it does not act when CPU crosses a level.
An alarm acts when its metric crosses a threshold, and that action can scale EC2 without anyone stepping in.
The metric tracks the CPU value, but on its own it never triggers an action when the value runs high.

steps.takeaway: An app's own error messages, gathered centrally and filtered by time, belong in CloudWatch Logs, not in metrics or CloudTrail.

read.text: CloudWatch Logs: central log storage and search.

steps.stem: During the lunch rush, some orders failed, and the cafe's ordering app wrote an error message for each one. The developers want to collect those messages in one place and filter them down to the lunch hour. Which should they use?

options.why: A metric tracks a numeric value over time, so it could count failed orders but cannot hold the text of each error message.
Insights flags unusual API activity in the account, which says nothing about the app's own failed orders.
CloudWatch Logs gathers an app's log files centrally, where the team can view, search and filter them.
CloudTrail logs hold records of API calls in the account, not the internal errors the ordering app reports.

incidents.title: The rota bucket left open overnight
incidents.brief: One morning the cafe's admin finds that the storage bucket holding the staff rotas was opened to the public during the night, and the owner wants to know how it happened and how to stop a repeat.

steps.takeaway: CloudTrail records refused requests as well as successful ones, each with its caller, time and IP address.

read.text: Who called, when, from which IP, and the result: a new state or a denial.

steps.stem: The cafe's admin thinks someone tried several times overnight to change the access settings on the staff rota bucket, and was refused before one try went through. She wants to see every try, refused or accepted, with who sent it and from which IP address. Which service fits?

options.why: CloudWatch tracks performance numbers and thresholds, not who called an API or what answer the call got.
Config checks resource settings against rules, and it does not list each refused request with its sender.
Trusted Advisor runs best-practice checks on the account, not a record of each request and who sent it.
CloudTrail records each request with its caller, time, IP address and result, whether a new state or a denial.

steps.takeaway: CloudTrail Insights learns normal API call volume and error rates, then flags unusual swings once you enable it.

read.text: CloudTrail Insights: spots abnormal API activity.

steps.stem: The cafe's admin wants AWS to learn how often API calls in the account usually fail, then flag any sudden rise in failed calls without her reading through the records herself. Which AWS CloudTrail feature should she turn on?

options.why: Event history lets her look up past management events, but it does not learn a normal error rate or flag a rise.
Insights studies normal API volume and error rates, then flags deviations once enabled on a trail or event data store.
Integrity validation exposes tampered log files, and it does not watch how often calls fail.
Log files keep events in S3 for long audits, but she would still read them herself, and they learn no normal error rate.

steps.takeaway: Recording resource settings over time and flagging any that break your own rules is the job of AWS Config.

read.text: AWS Config records configurations, tracks changes and checks them against your rules.

steps.stem: The cafe has a rule that its staff rota buckets must never be public. It wants a service that keeps a record of each bucket's settings as they change, checks them against that rule and alerts the admin about any bucket that breaks it. Which service fits?

options.why: Audit Manager gathers evidence that controls work, and it does not evaluate each bucket's settings against the rule.
CloudTrail records the API calls made in the account, but it does not judge resource settings against a rule.
Config records resource configurations, tracks their changes and flags any resource that breaks the cafe's rule.
Artifact hands out AWS's own audit reports and agreements, not checks of the cafe's bucket settings.

incidents.title: The bank's review before the coffee bar contract
incidents.brief: A bank offers the cafe a contract to run the coffee bar in its head office, but the bank's risk team first wants to review how the cafe keeps its cloud apps in line with the rules that bind it.

steps.takeaway: On AWS a business inherits compliant infrastructure, so its own compliance work centers on its own workloads and data.

read.text: You inherit AWS's best-practice data centers, networks, policies, processes and newest security controls.

steps.stem: The bank's risk team notices that the cafe's compliance checklist covers only its own apps and data, with no items for the servers, networks or buildings underneath. What explains the gap?

options.text: AWS leaves data in the Region the cafe picks
options.why: AWS does keep data in the chosen Region, but where data sits says nothing about who answers for the servers and buildings.

options.text: The cafe inherits AWS's audited infrastructure
options.why: The cafe inherits AWS's audited data centers, networks and controls, so its own checklist only needs its workloads and data.

options.text: AWS CloudTrail logs the API calls in the account
options.why: CloudTrail does record API calls, but a log of calls does not take the servers and buildings off the cafe's checklist.

options.text: Many AWS services let the cafe turn on encryption
options.why: Built-in encryption protects the cafe's data, yet it is one of the cafe's own tasks and does not explain the missing infrastructure items.

steps.takeaway: Compliance whitepapers and the auditing security checklist live in the Customer Compliance Center, not in AWS Artifact.

read.text: Its whitepapers cover key compliance questions, a risk and compliance overview, and an auditing security checklist.

steps.stem: To get ready for the bank's review, the cafe's operations lead wants AWS whitepapers that answer common regulatory questions, along with a checklist for auditing security. Where should she look?

options.why: Artifact Reports holds outside audit reports on AWS itself, not whitepapers with an auditing checklist.
Audit Manager gathers evidence about the cafe's own controls, and it is no library of compliance whitepapers.
Artifact Agreements is where the cafe reads and signs its agreements with AWS, not where whitepapers live.
The AWS Compliance Center, also called the Customer Compliance Center, holds whitepapers on key compliance questions and a checklist for auditing security.

steps.takeaway: AWS Audit Manager works with read-only access, so gathering audit evidence never changes the resources it checks.

read.text: Read-only access protects audit integrity, and it supports internal risk assessments.

steps.stem: The cafe uses AWS Audit Manager to gather proof for the bank's review. The bank's auditors worry that the tool itself might change the resources it inspects and spoil the audit. What answers their worry?

options.text: It collects evidence automatically across teams
options.why: Automated evidence collection is true of Audit Manager, but it says nothing about whether the tool changes what it inspects.

options.text: It maps resources to prebuilt standard frameworks
options.why: Prebuilt frameworks are a real Audit Manager feature, yet mapping resources to a standard does not show the tool leaves them unchanged.

options.text: It builds reports that are ready for auditors
options.why: Audit Manager does build audit-ready reports, but a report says nothing about whether gathering it altered the resources.

options.text: It uses read-only access to what it audits
options.why: Audit Manager reads the resources without changing them, and that read-only access protects the audit's integrity.

incidents.title: Bringing the airport kiosk into the fold
incidents.brief: The cafe's new airport kiosk has run on its own AWS account since a trial last spring, and the owner wants it held to the same standards as the cafe's other accounts before the holiday travel rush.

steps.takeaway: Bringing many accounts under one bill, one set of central controls and shared resources points to AWS Organizations.

read.text: One place to run billing, access, security and compliance for all accounts, and to share resources between them.

steps.stem: The cafe's airport kiosk runs on a standalone AWS account, apart from the cafe's other accounts. The owner wants its bill rolled up with theirs and its access, security and compliance run from the same central place, and she wants it able to use resources the other accounts share. Which service fits?

options.why: Service Catalog offers a curated list of approved resources, and it does not combine bills or run accounts centrally.
Artifact serves AWS's audit reports and agreements, and it does not group accounts or roll up their bills.
License Manager tracks and controls software licenses, not the billing and access of whole accounts.
Organizations runs billing, access, security and compliance for many accounts in one place and lets them share resources.

steps.takeaway: To cap one account and no other, attach the SCP to that member account, since an SCP on the root or an OU reaches every account beneath it.

read.text: SCPs cap permissions and attach only to OUs or member accounts.

steps.stem: The airport kiosk account has joined the cafe's organization and sits directly under the root, while the shop accounts sit in a shops OU and the office accounts in a back-office OU. The owner wants only the kiosk account capped to the few services it needs, even for its own admins, with every other account left as it is. Where should she attach the service control policy?

options.text: To the organization root above every account
options.why: An SCP on the root reaches every account in the organization, and the owner wants the other accounts left as they are.

options.text: To the kiosk's member account where it sits now
options.why: An SCP can attach to one member account, so it caps that account's users and roles, admins included, and no other account.

options.text: To the shops OU, after moving the kiosk into it
options.why: An SCP on the shops OU would cap the kiosk, but it would cap every shop account in that OU along with it.

options.text: To the back-office OU, after moving the kiosk into it
options.why: An SCP on the back-office OU would cap the kiosk, but it would cap every office account in that OU along with it.

steps.takeaway: In Trusted Advisor, red means action recommended, orange means investigation recommended and green means no problem found.

read.text: Status colors: red for action recommended, orange for investigation recommended, green for no problem found.

steps.stem: Before the holiday travel rush, the cafe's owner opens AWS Trusted Advisor for the airport kiosk's account. One of its checks shows an orange status. What does that status tell her?

options.why: Trusted Advisor marks a check red when it recommends action, so orange is one step short of that.

options.text: The check needs a higher support plan
options.why: The support plan sets how many checks an account gets, while a status color reports what a check found.
Orange is the status Trusted Advisor gives when it recommends looking into a finding before acting.
A check with no problem found shows green, not orange.
